newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African verdict thwarts "third force" theorists.
newsitem.headline: S.African verdict thwarts "third force" theorists.

text.p: The acquittal of apartheid-era defence minister Magnus Malan on murder charges has angered those South Africans who believe a mysterious "third force" orchestrated a decade of political bloodshed between blacks.
The country's Communist-aligned labour federation, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), said it was "extremely disappointed".

"While Cosatu accepts that the judge's verdict is based on the evidence placed in court, we feel that the judgement has far reaching negative consequences," said the union, which represents about 1.5 million people.
Judge Jan Hugo on Friday cleared Malan and 15 others of 13 murder charges arising from the massacre of black men, women and children in KwaMakutha settlement in KwaZulu-Natal province in 1987.
The massacre was one of many carried out since the mid-1980s in an orgy of violence in the province that has killed an estimated 15,000 blacks.

The protagonists were President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress and Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Inkatha Freedom Party. ANC leaders had hoped the Malan trial would prove that the apartheid government played midwife to the violence.

The judge said the KwaMakutha killing was almost certainly carried Inkatha members given military training by Malan's officers, but said this did not prove any conspiracy to murder by the government.te president and Malan's boss for several years, and by Buthelezi.
"It was not a criminal trial, it was a political trial by the ruling (ANC) party to try and destroy me and the IFP," said Buthelezi. "Justice was not only done, it was seen to be done."
De Klerk told a meeting of his National Party on Friday night that the ANC had much to answer for.
"The overwhelming majority of deaths as a result of political violence resulted from black on black violence."
"Unfortunately we have seen little effort to get to the bottom of the ANC's involvement in the conflict -- the massive intimidation, violence and necklace murders of black opponents."
President Mandela said after the verdict that South Africans should accept the judge's decision and that the hunt for apartheid's criminals would continue unabated.
But Cosatu said in its statement: "Today millions will ask whether there will ever be a successful prosecution of the third force elements who operated during the apartheid regime.
Archbishop Desmond Tutu, chairman of the country's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, said he believed the best way to uncover the truth of apartheid-era atrocities was through his commission.
It has the power to grant amnesty to perpetrators who confess freely. Malan maintained throughout his trial that he would not use the commission because he had nothing to confess.
